wine.name: Graffigna Centenario Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec alone, by a review of the 2007 vintage and the listings of later ones.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the Tulum Valley, the warm, dry valley floor around the city of San Juan, by the listings read; no single vineyard is named for it.
wine.making: By retailers' notes and reviews of several vintages, part of the wine, about half by one listing, was aged in oak barrels for around twelve months and the rest kept out of wood, and the two were blended before bottling, so the oak frames the fruit rather than leading it.
wine.glass: Ripe plum and blackberry with black pepper, liquorice and a vanilla edge from the oak aged part, juicy rather than taut, with soft, rounded tannin: the warm, generous manner of the Tulum Valley floor.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first few years, while the fruit is fresh; it was never a wine for long keeping.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Graffigna is the old name of San Juan wine, dated by the house to 1870, and its Centenario Malbec was the reserve red that carried it abroad: Tulum Valley Malbec, part of it aged in oak, ripe and soft, to pour young.
records.story: By its own history, the first vineyard under the Graffigna name was planted in San Juan in 1870; other accounts give 1869 for an uncle's purchase of land at Desamparados, or 1876 for the start of the founder's own cellar. The founder came from Italy as a youth, and by the house's account he followed the railway in the 1880s to reach new drinkers and was among the first in Argentina to sell wine under a brand. He died in 1923, on a journey to see his family in Italy. The cellar at Desamparados, with a museum named for him opened in 2003, became a stop for visitors to the province. The Centenario range gave the old name a reserve tier in its export years: its Malbec, from the Tulum Valley, was bottled under San Juan in the vintages of the 2000s and early 2010s. In January 2019 Pernod Ricard Argentina announced the sale of Graffigna, with its San Juan cellar and vineyards and a vineyard at La Consulta in the Uco Valley, to the Chilean VSPT Wine Group. In 2022, by trade reports, the house turned its range towards Uco Valley fruit in Mendoza, while keeping vineyards in San Juan. The Centenario is the taste of the San Juan Graffigna that came before that turn.

wine.name: Finca Las Moras Gran Syrah
wine.sites: A blend of three San Juan valleys, by the house's page: the warm Tulum Valley at about 650 metres, the Zonda Valley at about 800 metres and the cool, high Pedernal Valley at about 1,300 metres; the share of each moves with the vintage.
wine.making: Aged for eighteen months in new French and American oak barrels, by the house's own page, before the lots of the three valleys are blended and bottled; the house's page gives no further detail of the fermentation.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and black pepper wrapped in the vanilla and toast of new barrels, warm and full in the San Juan manner, with ripe, rounded tannin and a fresher finish from the Pedernal share.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it keeps for some years as the oak settles into the fruit.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a large Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Finca Las Moras puts three San Juan valleys into one bottle with its Gran Syrah: warm Tulum, Zonda and cool, high Pedernal Syrah, aged a year and a half in new French and American oak. An hour in a decanter readies it for the grill.
records.story: San Juan grew vines long before 1993, mostly for everyday wine, table grapes and concentrate. Finca Las Moras, named by two guides for the mulberry trees round its vineyards, dates itself to that year, when its Tulum Valley vineyards were restructured under the guidance of an Australian viticulturist, by two guides to the province's wineries. The work turned the house towards wines of quality at a time when the province was known for volume, and the guides count it among the pioneers of that turn. Syrah became its grape. The warm Tulum floor gave ripeness, and the house farmed in two valleys to the west as well: Zonda, at the foot of the Andean foothills, and Pedernal, high in the south, which its own pages call the coolest valley of the province. The Gran Syrah gathers all three, each valley at its own height, and spends eighteen months in new oak. Its 2011 vintage was reviewed by Decanter under San Juan, and in 2014 the same magazine's Argentina coverage carried a feature on the house in a province long seen as a bulk region. Where Mendoza made its name with Malbec, San Juan made its own with Syrah, and the Gran Syrah carries that grape with all its warmth.

wine.name: Callia Magna Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah, printed as Shiraz on some export labels.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyards in the Tulum Valley at Caucete, on poor alluvial soils of sandy loam with little organic matter, by its sheets, between the Pie de Palo range and the Cerro Chico of Zonda.
wine.making: By the house's sheet for the 2018 vintage, half of the wine was aged for nine months in barrels, split evenly between French and American oak, and the other half kept out of wood, before the two were blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Fig and cassis with a vanilla note from the barrels, by the house's own sheet; ripe and sweet on entry, warm and round, with soft tannin and the generous fruit of the Tulum Valley floor.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk within its first few years, while its ripe fruit leads; a few years more soften the oak.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a Bordeaux glass.

The valley round the city of San Juan where the house's vineyards and cellar lie.

records.table: Callia was built for Syrah: a Tulum Valley cellar at Caucete founded in 2002 by the family behind Bodegas Salentein. Its Magna Syrah, half of it aged nine months in French and American oak, shows fig and cassis, the warm San Juan style.
records.story: The Dutch family behind Bodegas Salentein of the Uco Valley founded Bodegas Callia in 2002, in the Tulum Valley at Caucete, east of the city of San Juan. The aim, in the house's own press kit, was to make the leading wines of San Juan and of Argentine Shiraz, and Syrah, the grape the province had made its name with, became its signature. Its vineyards lie on poor alluvial soils in a valley of very little rain, between the Pie de Palo range and the Cerro Chico of Zonda, and the press kit of 2014 also counts a large estate in the high Pedernal Valley to the south. The range runs from the everyday Alta and Bella bottlings to the Magna wines and the Grand Callia above them. The Magna Syrah keeps to Tulum fruit, with half the wine in oak, so it shows the warm valley floor rather than the mountains. The same family's Pyros wines come from the Pedernal Valley. By its sheet for the 2018 vintage, the Magna Syrah spent nine months in barrels split between French and American oak. Taste it beside a Pyros Malbec to hear the province's two climates, the valley floor and the heights.

wine.name: Pyros Single Vineyard Block No. 4 Malbec
wine.sites: The house's vineyard on the west slope of the Pedernal hill at about 1,400 metres, on very stony soils of limestone and flint; the 2021 sheet draws the wine from a polygon taking in parts of parcels 3, 4 and 5.
wine.making: By the house's sheet for 2021, macerated about four weeks after fermentation, then aged twelve months in barrels, mostly French and the rest American, about one in seven of them new and the rest second and third use; nine months more pass before release.
wine.glass: Blueberry, blackberry and sour cherry with wild flowers and dusty herbs, white pepper and a flinty edge; deep violet in colour, fresh and lifted rather than plush, by the house's note and reviews.
wine.ageing: Approachable after decanting on release, it has the structure and freshness to keep for several years more, by reviews of its vintages.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so; a large Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Pyros takes its Greek name for fire from the flints of the Pedernal Valley, and its Block No. 4 Malbec comes from one stony parcel at about 1,400 metres: perfumed, minty and fresh, a mountain answer to warm San Juan; let it breathe for an hour.
records.story: Pedernal is Spanish for flint, and the valley that bears the name lies high in the south of San Juan, the coolest of the province's valleys by a neighbouring house's account. In 2008 the Dutch founder of Bodegas Salentein began Pyros there, with a vineyard on the west slope of the Pedernal hill at about 1,400 metres; the vines were planted that year, by the house's sheets. The name, as the house tells it, comes from a local legend: struck together, the flints of the valley throw sparks, and the old people of the region lit their fires with them. Pyros is Greek for fire. The soils are stony, rich in limestone and flint, and the vineyard is farmed in numbered parcels. The Appellation Malbec gathers the estate; Block No. 4 is a small part of it bottled alone, the house's case for San Juan Malbec grown high. By the house's sheet for 2021 most of its barrels were second and third use, so the site leads rather than the oak. Down in the warm Tulum Valley the same family keeps its Callia cellar, so the pair spans the province from its floor to its heights.

wine.name: Cara Sur Criolla Chica
wine.grapes: Criolla Chica, the grape Chile calls País and the Canaries Listán Prieto, brought to the Americas by the Spanish.
wine.sites: Old vines trained on pergolas, the parral of the valley, in parcels around Barreal in the Calingasta Valley at the foot of the Andes, some eighty years old and more by importers' accounts.
wine.making: Fermented spontaneously with native yeasts on its skins in ovoid concrete, mostly destemmed, without temperature control by an importer's sheet, then aged in concrete for some months before bottling; the details move with the vintage.
wine.glass: Strawberry, red cherry and rose petal with cracked white pepper and a saline edge, pale cherry in colour, light in body, with gentle tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, within a few years of the vintage, while its red fruit is bright.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, lightly chilled; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The old mission grape of the Spanish, known in Chile as País.
Spanish for south face, after the harder southern face of Cerro Mercedario above Barreal.

records.table: Cara Sur, a tiny cellar at Barreal under the Andes, bottles Criolla Chica, the grape the Spanish brought, from old pergola vines of the Calingasta Valley. Pale, light and peppery, with strawberry and rose, it is served lightly chilled.
records.story: Barreal lies in the Calingasta Valley, high on the Andean side of San Juan, where smallholders kept old pergolas of Criolla grapes long after most of Argentina had turned to Malbec. Two couples began Cara Sur there. By one partner's telling they first made Criollas at university in 2008, then in a parents' garage in 2011, the year the project was formed. One partner is of the family behind Familia Zuccardi in Mendoza, but Cara Sur is a project of its own. The name means south face, for the harder southern route up Cerro Mercedario, a high Andean peak seen from Barreal. The tiny cellar stands beside two of the partners' homes, takes fruit from old vines of the valley, ferments with native yeasts in concrete and adds little else. Criolla Chica is the mission grape of the Spanish, País in Chile, and little of it is left in Argentina. Until 2024 the National Wine Institute counted it a pink grape, outside its list of varieties for quality wine; its Resolution 30 of 16 August 2024 added Criolla Chica, or Listán Prieto, to that list as a red. The bottle shows that old grape at altitude: light, fresh and its own.

traps: Criolla Chica is not Criolla Grande or Cereza, the pink skinned Criollas: it is the dark grape Chile calls País and the Canaries Listán Prieto.
Cara Sur is in the Calingasta Valley of San Juan, not in Mendoza, and it is a separate project from Familia Zuccardi.

report: No primary source: the house's own site was not searched within the share; every fact rests on two or more secondary sources, and the decree of 2024 on two trade reports.
The four founders are living and are not named; the partner of the Zuccardi family is described only as of the family behind Familia Zuccardi, wave one's Mendoza pick.
The label reads Criolla Chica on importers' and retailers' listings and Criolla on a Decanter review of 2021; the plan's word is kept inside the fuller name.

Vine ages differ (some eighty years on one importer page, a hundred years by another account); the record gives some eighty years by the importer's account. Whole bunch or destemmed differs by vintage and source.
The seven months in concrete is for one vintage, from a critic's guide quoted by a retailer.

The year a red of Criolla Chica could first be labelled as a quality wine, and what Cara Sur printed before 2024, were not confirmed: the record says only that a red of it stood outside the quality list.
Left out: the oldest of the Criolla family (one partner's quote only) and the planted area in Argentina (a figure, volatile).

story: was the institute's 'decree' and 'the partners pressed for change'; now Resolution 30 of 16 August 2024, which added Criolla Chica or Listán Prieto to the list of varieties for quality wine as a red, by the Boletín Oficial; the pressing for change cut, found in no source read.

others: La Totora was 'vines planted in 1930 on alluvial soils of quartz'; now old vines near Barreal, part whole bunch, on its lees in a concrete egg, since one merchant gives 1930 to a different vineyard, Finca Maggio.
